import pandas as pd


DESCRIPTION = "Mean reversion: buy when the price is cheap relative to its normal range (z-score)."

N_TRIALS = 1
PARAM_GRID = None


def run(prices: pd.DataFrame, entry: float = -0.5) -> pd.Series:
    c = prices["close"]
    z = (c - c.mean()) / c.std()
    signal = (z < entry).astype(float)
    return signal.shift(1).fillna(0.0)

plan.strategy_summary: The strategy goes long when the z‑score of the closing price falls below a threshold (entry), indicating the price is cheap relative to its historical average, and stays flat otherwise.

findings.explanation: Uses the full‑sample mean and standard deviation, which incorporate future close prices into the z‑score.

test_plan.hypothesis: Adding an extra shift does not remove the future‑dependent mean/std, so performance remains similar.
Because the z‑score uses the global mean and std, truncating the series alters those statistics and changes the signal.
No parameter grid is defined, so the walk‑forward test is not applicable.
Since only one configuration is tested, the deflation adjustment is minimal; on random‑walk data the Sharpe will be near zero, triggering a warning.

import pandas as pd

DESCRIPTION = "Mean reversion: buy when the price is cheap relative to its normal range (z-score)."

N_TRIALS = 1
PARAM_GRID = None

def run(prices: pd.DataFrame, entry: float = -0.5) -> pd.Series:
    c = prices["close"]
    window = 20
    mean = c.rolling(window, min_periods=1).mean().shift(1)
    std = c.rolling(window, min_periods=1).std().shift(1)
    std = std.replace(0, 1e-9)
    z = (c - mean) / std
    signal = (z < entry).astype(float)
    return signal.shift(1).fillna(0.0)
